summary.text: For \(1\le k<60\), an explicit finite table supplies prime decompositions of \(4k+2\); for \(k\ge60\), set \(n=2k+1>120\) and use the assumed nonzero determinant. A nonzero determinant forces the zeroth row to contain a \(1\), so for some \(j<n\), both \(n-j\) and \(n+j\) are prime, and their sum is \(2n=4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement for A228623: for every odd integer \(n>120\), the determinant \(a(n)\) is nonzero. We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the integer \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

For a positive integer \(n\), let \(M_n\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), and whose \((i,j)\)-entry is
\[
 (M_n)_{i,j}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n-i+j\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the expressions are nonnegative: since \(i,j<n\), one has \(n+i\ge j+1\) and \(n+j\ge i+1\). Thus the natural-number subtractions in these expressions agree with ordinary integer subtraction. By definition, \(a(n)=\det M_n\).

Fix \(k>0\). We divide the proof into the cases \(k<60\) and \(k\ge 60\).

First suppose \(1\le k<60\). The required decompositions are given explicitly in the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
 k&4k+2&&k&4k+2&&k&4k+2\\ \hline
 1&6=3+3&&21&86=3+83&&41&166=3+163\\
 2&10=3+7&&22&90=7+83&&42&170=3+167\\
 3&14=3+11&&23&94=5+89&&43&174=7+167\\
 4&18=5+13&&24&98=19+79&&44&178=5+173\\
 5&22=3+19&&25&102=5+97&&45&182=3+179\\
 6&26=3+23&&26&106=3+103&&46&186=5+181\\
 7&30=7+23&&27&110=3+107&&47&190=11+179\\
 8&34=3+31&&28&114=5+109&&48&194=3+191\\
 9&38=7+31&&29&118=5+113&&49&198=5+193\\
10&42=5+37&&30&122=13+109&&50&202=3+199\\
11&46=3+43&&31&126=13+113&&51&206=7+199\\
12&50=3+47&&32&130=3+127&&52&210=11+199\\
13&54=7+47&&33&134=3+131&&53&214=3+211\\
14&58=5+53&&34&138=7+131&&54&218=7+211\\
15&62=3+59&&35&142=3+139&&55&222=11+211\\
16&66=5+61&&36&146=7+139&&56&226=3+223\\
17&70=3+67&&37&150=11+139&&57&230=3+227\\
18&74=3+71&&38&154=3+151&&58&234=5+229\\
19&78=5+73&&39&158=7+151&&59&238=5+233\\
20&82=3+79&&40&162=5+157&&&
\end{array}
\]
Every summand displayed in this table is prime. This is a finite trial-division check: the largest summand is \(233\), and any composite integer at most \(233\) has a prime divisor no greater than \(\sqrt{233}<16\). It therefore suffices, apart from the small primes themselves, to test divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\); the displayed numbers pass the relevant tests. The equalities in the table are immediate additions. Consequently the conclusion holds for every positive \(k<60\).

Now suppose \(k\ge 60\), and set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd. Moreover,
\[
 n=2k+1\ge 2\cdot 60+1=121>120.
\]
The assumed conjecture therefore applies and gives
\[
 \det M_n=a(n)\ne 0.
\]

Consider the row of \(M_n\) indexed by \(i=0\). A matrix with an identically zero row has determinant zero: for example, in the permutation expansion of its determinant, every product contains one entry from that row and is therefore zero. Since \(\det M_n\ne0\), the row indexed by \(0\) cannot be identically zero. Hence there is some column index \(j\), with
\[
 0\le j<n,
\]
for which
\[
 (M_n)_{0,j}\ne0.
\]
All entries of \(M_n\) are either \(0\) or \(1\), so this entry is in fact \(1\). By the definition of the matrix entry, both numbers
\[
 n+0-j=n-j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 n-0+j=n+j
\]
are prime. Define
\[
 p=n-j,\qquad q=n+j.
\]
The inequality \(j<n\) ensures that \(n-j\) is an ordinary nonnegative (indeed positive) difference, so there is no truncation issue. We have just proved that both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. Finally,
\[
 p+q=(n-j)+(n+j)=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is the sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\).

The finite table handles all \(1\le k<60\), while the determinant argument handles every \(k\ge60\). Therefore, under the conjectured nonvanishing of \(a(n)\) for odd \(n>120\), every integer of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes.
